lessons.title: Supply and Demand Fundamentals
lessons.focus: Introduces the law of demand, law of supply, market equilibrium, and price mechanisms.

data.title: Supply and Demand Fundamentals
data.summary: This lesson explains the basic laws of demand and supply, how they interact to create market equilibrium, and how prices adjust. Students will see how these ideas shape everyday market decisions.
objectives: Define the law of demand and the law of supply
Draw and interpret demand and supply curves
Identify the market equilibrium point
Explain how price changes signal shortages or surpluses
Calculate equilibrium price and quantity from simple data
data.prerequisites: Students should know the meaning of a market and have basic graph‑reading skills; no prior economics knowledge is required.
why: Understanding demand and supply helps people predict how prices will react to changes such as a new technology or a seasonal shortage, which is useful for personal budgeting and business planning.
Governments and firms use these concepts to set policies, decide production levels, and evaluate the impact of taxes or subsidies on the economy.

sections.heading: 1. The Law of Demand
sections.body:
The law of demand says that, **ceteris paribus**, when the price of a good goes up, the amount people want to buy (the quantity demanded) goes down.  
*“Ceteris paribus”* is a Latin phrase that means “all other things being equal.” It tells us to hold everything else constant—income, tastes, the price of other goods, etc.—so we can see the pure effect of the price change.

> **Definition:** *Law of Demand* – a higher price leads to a lower quantity demanded, assuming all other factors stay the same.

Why does this happen?  
1. **Budget constraint** – People have limited money. If a product becomes more expensive, they can afford to buy less of it.  
2. **Substitution effect** – When the price of one good rises, consumers tend to switch to cheaper alternatives.  
3. **Diminishing marginal utility** – The more of a good you already have, the less extra satisfaction (utility) each additional unit gives you. When the price rises, the extra satisfaction is not worth the higher cost, so you buy less.

Think of a simple everyday comparison: imagine you love buying chocolate bars for $1 each. One day the shop raises the price to $2. With the same pocket money, you can only buy half as many bars, so you either buy fewer bars or look for a cheaper snack. The change in your buying behaviour illustrates the law of demand.

> **In daily life:** When gasoline prices increase, many drivers drive fewer miles or choose public transport, showing a lower quantity demanded for fuel.

### From words to a simple formula

Economists often write the relationship between price ($P$) and quantity demanded ($Q_d$) as:

$$ Q_d = f(P) $$

where $f$ is a decreasing function: as $P$ rises, $f(P)$ falls. In a straight‑line (linear) approximation we can write:

$$ Q_d = a - bP $$

Here:
- $a$ is the quantity demanded when price is zero (the intercept).  
- $b$ is a positive number that tells us how much quantity falls when price rises by one unit (the slope).

Because $b>0$, the slope $-b$ is negative, confirming that the curve slopes downward.

### Worked example – coffee shop latte

**Example 1 (Easy): Latte price change**

A coffee shop raises the price of a latte from \$3 to \$4 and sells 20 fewer lattes per day.  
How much does the quantity demanded change for each \$1 increase in price?  

1. **Identify the change in price** – subtract the old price from the new price.  
   $$ \Delta P = 4 - 3 = 1\ \text{dollar} $$
2. **Identify the change in quantity demanded** – subtract the new quantity from the old quantity (the problem tells us the drop is 20 lattes).  
   $$ \Delta Q_d = -20\ \text{lattes} $$
3. **Compute the slope $b$** – the change in quantity per one‑dollar change in price.  
   $$ b = -\frac{\Delta Q_d}{\Delta P} = -\frac{-20}{1} = 20 $$

**Answer:** For each \$1 increase in the latte price, the coffee shop sells 20 fewer lattes per day. The negative sign in $\Delta Q_d$ shows a decrease, matching the law of demand.

### Interpreting the result

The slope $b = 20$ tells us the **price sensitivity** of latte buyers at this shop. If the shop raised the price by \$2, we would expect roughly $2 \times 20 = 40$ fewer lattes sold, assuming the linear relationship holds and no other factors change.

> **Note:** The law of demand describes a *relationship*, not a fixed rule. Real markets may show exceptions (e.g., luxury goods where higher price can increase prestige and demand), but those cases involve other factors changing, so the “ceteris paribus” condition is violated.

### Graphical intuition (without drawing)

Imagine a graph with price on the vertical axis and quantity demanded on the horizontal axis. The line $Q_d = a - bP$ starts high on the quantity axis (when price is low) and slopes down to the right. Moving rightward (higher quantity) forces you down to a lower price point; moving upward (higher price) forces you leftward to a lower quantity. This visual slope is exactly what the equation $-b$ tells us.

### Why the law matters

Understanding that higher prices reduce quantity demanded helps businesses set prices, governments predict tax impacts, and consumers anticipate how market changes affect their spending. For instance, if a city imposes a tax that raises the price of movie tickets, the law of demand predicts fewer tickets will be sold, which can affect cinema revenues and even local employment.

> **Remember:** The law of demand holds only when *all other influences* (income, tastes, prices of related goods) stay the same. If any of those change, the observed quantity may move for reasons other than price.

### Quick check

Suppose a bakery lowers the price of a muffin from \$2 to \$1.5 and observes that sales rise from 80 muffins to 100 muffins per day. Using the same steps as the latte example, the slope would be:

1. $\Delta P = 1.5 - 2 = -0.5$ dollars  
2. $\Delta Q_d = 100 - 80 = 20$ muffins  
3. $b = -\frac{20}{-0.5} = 40$

The positive $b$ (40) again confirms that a price drop leads to a quantity increase, consistent with the law of demand.

By mastering this simple relationship, you are ready to explore how supply works and how the two together determine market outcomes.

sections.heading: 2. The Law of Supply
sections.body:
The law of supply says that, **ceteris paribus** (​*all other things being equal*​), producers are willing to offer more of a good when its price rises, and less when its price falls.  

> **Definition:** *Law of Supply* – a positive relationship between the price of a product and the quantity that producers are ready to sell, holding everything else constant.  

Why does this happen?  
1. **Higher revenue potential** – If the market price goes up, each unit sold brings in more money. That extra revenue can cover higher costs (like labor or raw materials) and still leave a profit.  
2. **Incentive to use resources** – Producers have limited resources (land, machines, workers). A higher price makes it worthwhile to shift those resources toward the profitable good and away from less‑profitable activities.  
3. **Covering higher marginal costs** – As a firm produces more, the cost of producing each additional unit (the *marginal cost*) usually rises. A higher price is needed to make those extra units profitable.

Think of a lemonade stand. When the price is $1 per cup, the student running the stand might sell 20 cups a day and earn $20. If the price rises to $2 per cup, the same student can earn $40 by selling the same 20 cups, or they might decide to make more lemonade to earn even more. The extra profit motivates them to buy more lemons, sugar, and maybe a larger pitcher.  

> **In daily life:** A baker sees the price of bread go up from \$2 to \$3 per loaf. Because each loaf now brings in an extra \$1, the baker decides to bake 20% more loaves each morning.

### From words to a simple formula  

Economists often write the supply relationship as  

$$ Q_s = f(P) $$  

where  

* $Q_s$ = quantity supplied (how many units producers are ready to sell)  
* $P$ = market price of the good  
* $f$ = a function that shows how $Q_s$ changes when $P$ changes, holding other factors constant.

If we assume a straight‑line (linear) supply curve, the function can be written as  

$$ Q_s = a + bP $$  

* $a$ is the quantity supplied when price is zero (often a negative number, showing that producers would not supply anything at a zero price).  
* $b$ is the *slope* of the supply curve; because the law of supply says the curve slopes upward, $b$ is a positive number.

### Worked example – how a price rise changes a farmer’s planting decision  

**Example 2 (Easy): Tomato farmer reacts to a price increase**  

A farmer receives \$2 more per kilogram of tomatoes. As a result, the farmer decides to plant 15 % more acres for tomatoes.  

1. **Identify the percentage change in quantity supplied.**  
   The farmer’s “quantity supplied” in this case is the area planted. A 15 % increase means  

   $$ \Delta Q_s\% = 15\% $$  

2. **Relate the percentage change to the price change.**  
   The price increase is \$2 per kilogram. To see the *price elasticity of supply* (how responsive supply is), we use  

   $$ \text{Elasticity} = \frac{\Delta Q_s\%}{\Delta P\%} $$  

   First find the percentage change in price. Suppose the original price was \$4/kg, so  

   $$ \Delta P\% = \frac{2}{4}\times 100\% = 50\% $$  

3. **Calculate the elasticity.**  
   $$ \text{Elasticity} = \frac{15\%}{50\%} = 0.30 $$  

**Answer:** The farmer’s supply of tomatoes is relatively inelastic (elasticity = 0.30). A \$2 price rise leads to a modest 15 % increase in planted acres.

The steps show how a higher price encourages the farmer to use more land, but the response is not huge because other factors (like limited land or labor) restrict how much more can be supplied.

### What the example tells us  

* The positive sign of the elasticity confirms the law of supply: quantity supplied rises when price rises.  
* The magnitude (0.30) tells us the response is small; producers may be constrained by resources, technology, or risk.  

> **Note:** Elasticity is a *ratio*; it tells us the size of the response, not just its direction.

### When the law does not hold  

The phrase *ceteris paribus* is crucial. If something else changes at the same time, the simple upward‑sloping relationship can break down. Examples:  

* **Input price rise** – If the cost of fertilizer doubles, the farmer may cut back even though tomato prices are higher.  
* **Regulatory limits** – A government may cap the amount of land that can be used for a crop, preventing the farmer from expanding.  

These are called *shifts* of the supply curve (the whole curve moves) rather than *movements* along the curve (a change in quantity supplied because of a price change).  

### Quick check – think of a coffee shop  

Suppose a coffee shop sells a cup of coffee for \$3 and sells 100 cups a day. If the price rises to \$4, the shop could earn an extra \$100 per day *if* it sold the same 100 cups. Because the extra profit looks attractive, the shop may decide to open earlier, hire an extra barista, and try to sell 120 cups. The increase from 100 to 120 cups is a *movement* along the supply curve caused by the higher price.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that a higher price always means producers will supply *infinitely* more. In reality, the upward slope is limited by resources, technology, and other costs.

### Summarizing the law  

* **Higher price → higher quantity supplied** (ceteris paribus).  
* The relationship is captured by an upward‑sloping supply curve, often written $Q_s = a + bP$ with $b>0$.  
* The *elasticity of supply* measures how strong the response is; values greater than 1 are “elastic,” less than 1 are “inelastic.”  
* Real‑world constraints can shift the whole curve, turning a price change into a smaller or larger effect.

Understanding the law of supply helps us predict how producers will react to market signals, and it sets the stage for later topics like market equilibrium and policy analysis.

sections.heading: 3. Drawing Demand and Supply Curves
sections.body:
The first thing to understand is **what a graph does**: it turns numbers into a picture that we can read at a glance.  
When we talk about markets, the two numbers we care about most are **price** (how much money is paid for one unit of a good) and **quantity** (how many units are bought or sold).  

> **Definition:** *Price* is the amount of money required to purchase one unit of a product.  
> **Definition:** *Quantity* is the number of units of a product that are bought or sold.

---

### 1. Setting up the axes  

1. **Choose the vertical axis (the y‑axis) for price.**  
   - We put price on the vertical line because we usually think of price as the “height” of a market condition – higher price means the line goes up.  
2. **Choose the horizontal axis (the x‑axis) for quantity.**  
   - Quantity runs left‑to‑right, just like distance on a road map.  

The point where the two axes cross is called the **origin** (0, 0). It represents a situation where both price and quantity are zero – a market that does not exist yet.

> **Note:** The scale on each axis can be chosen freely, but it must be consistent (e.g., $1 increments for price, 10‑unit increments for quantity).

---

### 2. Plotting a demand curve  

The **law of demand** tells us that, all else equal, consumers buy more when the price is lower. This creates a **downward‑sloping** line on our graph.

**Steps to plot a demand curve**

1. List a few price‑quantity pairs that follow the demand rule.  
2. Mark each pair as a point on the graph: the price tells you how high to go, the quantity tells you how far to the right.  
3. Connect the points with a smooth line; the line should slope downwards from left to right.

#### Worked Example 3 (Medium): Coffee demand  

*Question:* A coffee shop finds that when the price is $2 per cup, 120 cups are sold each day. If the price rises to $4, only 80 cups are sold. Plot the demand curve using these two points.

1. **Write the two price‑quantity pairs.**  
   $$ (P_1, Q_1) = (2,\;120) $$  
   $$ (P_2, Q_2) = (4,\;80) $$
2. **Mark the points on the graph.**  
   - For $(2,120)$ go up to the $2$ mark on the vertical axis, then move right to the $120$ mark on the horizontal axis.  
   - For $(4,80)$ go up to $4$ on the vertical axis, then right to $80$ on the horizontal axis.
3. **Draw a straight line through the two points.** Because demand is assumed linear in this simple example, the line connecting them represents the whole demand curve.

**Answer:** The demand curve is a straight line that passes through $(2,120)$ and $(4,80)$, sloping downwards as price increases.

---

### 3. Plotting a supply curve  

The **law of supply** says producers are willing to sell more when the price is higher. This creates an **upward‑sloping** line.

**Steps to plot a supply curve**

1. Gather price‑quantity pairs that follow the supply rule.  
2. Plot each pair on the same axes as before.  
3. Connect the points; the line should rise from left to right.

#### Worked Example 4 (Medium): Tomato supply  

*Question:* A farmer can bring 30 kilograms of tomatoes to market when the price is $1 per kilogram, and 70 kilograms when the price is $3 per kilogram. Plot the supply curve.

1. **Write the two price‑quantity pairs.**  
   $$ (P_1, Q_1) = (1,\;30) $$  
   $$ (P_2, Q_2) = (3,\;70) $$
2. **Mark the points on the graph.**  
   - For $(1,30)$ go up to $1$ on the vertical axis, then right to $30$ on the horizontal axis.  
   - For $(3,70)$ go up to $3$ on the vertical axis, then right to $70$ on the horizontal axis.
3. **Draw a straight line through the two points.** Because we assume a linear supply relationship, the line connecting them is the supply curve.

**Answer:** The supply curve is a straight line through $(1,30)$ and $(3,70)$, sloping upwards as price rises.

---

### 4. Putting demand and supply together  

Now we place **both** curves on the same set of axes. The point where they intersect is called the **market equilibrium** – the price and quantity where what consumers want to buy exactly equals what producers want to sell.

> **In daily life:** Think of a busy farmers’ market. If the price of strawberries is too low, sellers run out quickly (shortage). If it is too high, many strawberries stay unsold (surplus). The price that clears the market is the equilibrium.

#### Worked Example 5 (Medium): Plotting both curves together  

*Question:* Using the coffee demand points $(2,120)$ and $(4,80)$ and the tomato supply points $(1,30)$ and $(3,70)$, draw both curves on the same graph and identify the intersection (if any).

1. **Draw the axes** with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.  
2. **Plot the two demand points** and connect them with a downward‑sloping line (as done in Example 3).  
3. **Plot the two supply points** and connect them with an upward‑sloping line (as done in Example 4).  
4. **Locate the intersection.** Because the demand points are at higher quantities (80–120) than the supply points (30–70), the two lines do **not** cross within the plotted range. This tells us that, with these particular numbers, the coffee market and the tomato market are unrelated; we would need additional points or a different good to find a true equilibrium.

**Answer:** The demand and supply lines do not intersect in the displayed range, indicating no common price‑quantity pair for these two separate goods. In practice, we would plot demand and supply for the *same* product to find equilibrium.

---

### 5. Why the graph matters  

A graph lets us see instantly:

- **How sensitive** quantity is to price changes (the steepness of the line).  
- **Where shortages or surpluses** would appear (areas above or below the equilibrium).  
- **What happens** if something shifts the curve (e.g., a new tax moves the supply curve upward).

> **Remember:** The vertical axis is always price, the horizontal axis is always quantity. Keeping this convention avoids confusion when you compare many markets.

By mastering the simple act of drawing these two lines, you gain a visual tool that economists use to explain almost every market phenomenon.

sections.heading: 4. Market Equilibrium
sections.body:
When buyers and sellers meet in a market, each side has its own wishes.  
Buyers want to purchase a certain amount of a good at a price they are willing to pay – this is the **quantity demanded**.  
Sellers are ready to offer a certain amount at a price they are willing to accept – this is the **quantity supplied**.  

If the price is too high, sellers will want to sell more than buyers want to buy, creating a **surplus**.  
If the price is too low, buyers will want more than sellers are ready to provide, creating a **shortage**.  

The market solves this problem by moving the price until the two quantities become exactly the same. The point where **quantity demanded equals quantity supplied** is called **market equilibrium**.

> **Definition:** *Market equilibrium* is the price‑quantity pair at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.

Why does this matter?  
When the market is at equilibrium, there is no pressure for the price to change. No one is left with unsold goods, and no one is turned away because the good is too expensive. This makes the market efficient – resources are used where they are most valued.

### Visualising equilibrium on a graph  

1. **Draw the axes** – the vertical axis (y‑axis) shows price (P), the horizontal axis (x‑axis) shows quantity (Q).  
2. **Plot the demand curve** – it slopes downward because, all else equal, a lower price makes buyers want more (the law of demand).  
3. **Plot the supply curve** – it slopes upward because a higher price encourages sellers to produce more (the law of supply).  
4. **Find the intersection** – the point where the two lines cross is the equilibrium. The price coordinate of this point is the **equilibrium price (Pe)**, and the quantity coordinate is the **equilibrium quantity (Qe)**.

At this crossing, the market “balances” – the two forces are equal and opposite, just like a seesaw that is perfectly level.

### Finding equilibrium algebraically  

When the demand and supply relationships are given as equations, we can solve for the equilibrium by setting them equal to each other:

$$ Q_d(P) = Q_s(P) $$

where $Q_d(P)$ is the demand function and $Q_s(P)$ is the supply function. Solving this equation gives the equilibrium price $P_e$. Substituting $P_e$ back into either the demand or supply equation yields the equilibrium quantity $Q_e$.

> **Note:** The algebraic method works for any linear or non‑linear functions, as long as you can solve the equation for $P$.

#### Worked example

**Example 4 (Medium): Solving for equilibrium price and quantity**  
Given the demand function $Q_d = 100 - 5P$ and the supply function $Q_s = 20 + 3P$, find the equilibrium price and quantity.

1. **Set demand equal to supply.**  
   $$ 100 - 5P = 20 + 3P $$

2. **Collect the $P$ terms on one side and constants on the other.**  
   Subtract $3P$ from both sides:  
   $$ 100 - 8P = 20 $$  
   Then subtract $20$ from both sides:  
   $$ 80 - 8P = 0 $$

3. **Solve for $P$.**  
   Add $8P$ to both sides:  
   $$ 80 = 8P $$  
   Divide by $8$:  
   $$ P = 10 $$  

   This $P$ is the equilibrium price $P_e$.

4. **Find the equilibrium quantity.**  
   Substitute $P = 10$ into either the demand or supply equation (they give the same result). Using demand:  
   $$ Q_e = 100 - 5(10) = 100 - 50 = 50 $$  

**Answer:** The market equilibrium is a price of **$10** and a quantity of **50 units**. At this price, buyers want exactly 50 units and sellers are willing to provide exactly 50 units.

### What equilibrium tells us about the market  

- **Stability:** If the price is above $P_e$, a surplus appears. Sellers lower the price to clear excess stock, moving the market back toward $P_e$.  
- **Instability:** If the price is below $P_e$, a shortage appears. Buyers compete for the limited goods, pushing the price up toward $P_e$.

> **In daily life:** Think of a farmer’s market where the price of strawberries settles at $3 per basket. At that price, the farmer brings exactly the number of baskets that shoppers are ready to buy. If the farmer tried $4 per basket, baskets would sit unsold (a surplus). If the price were $2, shoppers would line up and the farmer would run out (a shortage). The $3 price is the equilibrium.

### Quick checklist for finding equilibrium  

1. Write down the demand and supply equations.  
2. Set them equal to each other and solve for $P$.  
3. Plug the resulting $P$ back into either equation to get $Q$.  
4. Verify that the same $Q$ comes from both equations – this confirms the solution.

> **Remember:** Equilibrium is a *point*, not a range. It is the unique price‑quantity pair where the two curves intersect (unless the curves are parallel, in which case no equilibrium exists).

Understanding equilibrium gives you a powerful tool: you can predict how changes—like a new tax, a subsidy, or a shift in consumer taste—will move the price and quantity away from the original balance, and then see how the market will respond to restore a new equilibrium. This foundation will be essential when we later discuss how policies affect real markets.

sections.heading: 5. Price Mechanisms: Shortages and Surpluses
sections.body:
When the price in a market is **not** at the point where the amount that buyers want to buy equals the amount that sellers want to sell, the market experiences either a **shortage** or a **surplus**.  

A **shortage** happens when the price is **too low**. At that price, many consumers want to buy the good, but producers are not willing to supply enough of it.  

A **surplus** happens when the price is **too high**. At that price, producers are eager to sell a lot, but consumers do not want to buy as much.

Why does this matter?  Prices act like signals. When a shortage appears, the signal tells producers “you could earn more if you raised the price,” and it tells consumers “there isn’t enough of the good, you may have to wait or look for alternatives.”  When a surplus appears, the signal tells producers “you are making too many units, lower the price,” and it tells consumers “there is plenty available, you can buy more if you want.”  These adjustments push the market back toward **equilibrium**, the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

### Everyday comparison
Think of a popular concert ticket. If the ticket price is set very low, more people want tickets than there are seats – a shortage. The organizer will quickly raise the price or add extra shows. If the price is set very high, many seats stay empty – a surplus. The organizer will lower the price or offer discounts. In both cases the price moves in the direction that reduces the mismatch.

### Step‑by‑step reasoning

1. **Identify the current price** and compare it with the **equilibrium price** (the price where the demand curve meets the supply curve).  
2. **Calculate quantity demanded** at that price using the demand equation.  
3. **Calculate quantity supplied** at that price using the supply equation.  
4. **Compare the two quantities**:  
   - If *quantity demanded* > *quantity supplied*, the market has a **shortage** of size  
     $$\text{Shortage} = Q_D - Q_S.$$  
   - If *quantity supplied* > *quantity demanded*, the market has a **surplus** of size  
     $$\text{Surplus} = Q_S - Q_D.$$

> **Definition:** *Shortage* = excess demand; *Surplus* = excess supply.  

> **Note:** The size of a shortage or surplus is measured in the same units as the good (e.g., units, kilograms, tickets).

### Worked Example 5 (Hard): Shortage or surplus at a given price  

**Question:** In the previous lesson we had the demand function $Q_D = 20 - 2P$ and the supply function $Q_S = 4P$. If the price is set at $6, calculate the resulting shortage or surplus.

1. **Find quantity demanded at $P = 6$**  
   $$Q_D = 20 - 2(6) = 20 - 12 = 8.$$  

2. **Find quantity supplied at $P = 6$**  
   $$Q_S = 4(6) = 24.$$  

3. **Compare the two quantities**  
   Since $Q_S > Q_D$, there is a surplus.  
   $$\text{Surplus} = Q_S - Q_D = 24 - 8 = 16.$$  

**Answer:** At a price of $6, the market has a surplus of **16 units**.

### How the market reacts
When a surplus appears, sellers lower their price to attract more buyers. As the price falls, the demand curve tells us that more consumers will want the good (quantity demanded rises), while the supply curve tells us that producers will be willing to sell fewer units (quantity supplied falls). The price keeps moving until the surplus disappears and the market reaches equilibrium again.

### Worked Example 6 (Hard): Price ceiling creates a shortage  

**Question:** Suppose the government imposes a price ceiling of $1 on the same market (demand $Q_D = 20 - 2P$, supply $Q_S = 4P$). Show how this creates a shortage and compute its size.

1. **Apply the price ceiling:** the maximum legal price is $P = 1$.  

2. **Calculate quantity demanded at $P = 1$**  
   $$Q_D = 20 - 2(1) = 20 - 2 = 18.$$  

3. **Calculate quantity supplied at $P = 1$**  
   $$Q_S = 4(1) = 4.$$  

4. **Determine the mismatch**  
   Because $Q_D > Q_S$, a shortage occurs.  
   $$\text{Shortage} = Q_D - Q_S = 18 - 4 = 14.$$  

**Answer:** The $1 price ceiling creates a shortage of **14 units**.

> **In daily life:** A price ceiling is like a rent‑control rule that says landlords cannot charge more than a set amount. If the ceiling is below the market rent, there are more people wanting apartments than apartments available – a shortage.

### Why the price moves automatically
If the price is above equilibrium, sellers notice unsold inventory and lower the price to clear it. If the price is below equilibrium, buyers find the good hard to obtain, and sellers can raise the price because buyers are willing to pay more. This “price mechanism” is the invisible hand that coordinates millions of individual decisions without any central planner.

> **Remember:** The market always pushes the price toward the point where *quantity demanded = quantity supplied*. Shortages push prices up; surpluses push prices down.

### Quick checklist for identifying shortages and surpluses  

| Step | Action | What you look for |
|------|--------|-------------------|
| 1 | Write down the current price $P$ | Given or imposed by policy |
| 2 | Compute $Q_D$ using the demand equation | How much buyers want |
| 3 | Compute $Q_S$ using the supply equation | How much sellers offer |
| 4 | Compare $Q_D$ and $Q_S$ | $Q_D > Q_S$ → shortage; $Q_S > Q_D$ → surplus |
| 5 | Calculate the size | Subtract the smaller from the larger |

Understanding these price mechanisms helps you predict what will happen when governments intervene, when technology changes production costs, or when consumer tastes shift. The next lesson will show how the whole curves shift, not just move along a single curve.

sections.heading: 6. Shifts vs. Movements
sections.body:
The idea of a **shift** versus a **movement** is simple once we separate two things that often get mixed up: the *price* of a good and the *other factors* that affect how much of it buyers want or sellers are willing to offer.

> **Definition:** A **movement** is a change **along** the same demand (or supply) curve caused only by a change in the price of the good.  
> **Definition:** A **shift** is a change of the **whole** demand (or supply) curve caused by a change in any other factor – for demand, things like income, tastes, or the price of related goods; for supply, things like technology, input prices, or the number of sellers.

Why does this matter?  If we know whether a price change is moving us along a curve or moving the curve itself, we can predict what will happen to the equilibrium price and quantity.  Policy makers, businesses, and consumers all use this knowledge to decide whether to raise wages, subsidize production, or change advertising.

### Step‑by‑step picture

1. **Start with one curve.**  
   Imagine a straight‑line demand curve: $Q_d = 100 - 2P$, where $Q_d$ is quantity demanded and $P$ is price.

2. **Change the price only.**  
   If the price falls from $P=20$ to $P=15$, we plug the new price into the same equation:  
   $$Q_d = 100 - 2(15) = 70.$$  
   The curve has not moved; we have simply moved to a new point **along** the same line.  

3. **Change something else (e.g., income).**  
   Suppose consumers become richer and now want to buy more at every price. The demand equation becomes $Q_d = 120 - 2P$. The whole line slides rightward; every price now corresponds to a larger quantity. This is a **shift** of the demand curve.

> **In daily life:** Think of a bus route (the curve). If the bus runs faster (price change), you simply get to a different stop on the same route (movement). If the city adds a new bus line that goes through more neighborhoods (shift), the whole route changes.

### How to tell the difference on a graph

- **Movement:** The point slides up or down the same line. The slope (steepness) stays the same.
- **Shift:** The entire line moves left or right (for demand) or up or down (for supply). The slope stays the same, but the intercept changes.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that any change in quantity bought or sold is a shift. Remember: only a change in a non‑price factor moves the whole curve.

### Worked Example – Demand Shift from Higher Income

**Example 8 (Hard): Income rise shifts demand right**

*Question:* If consumer income rises, demand shifts right to $Q_d = 120 - 5P$. Find the new equilibrium with the original supply curve $Q_s = 20 + 3P$.

**Steps**

1. **Write down the new demand equation** (already given).  
   $$Q_d = 120 - 5P$$

2. **Set demand equal to supply** to find the equilibrium where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers want.  
   $$120 - 5P = 20 + 3P$$

3. **Solve for the price $P$**.  
   - Bring the $P$ terms to one side:  
     $$120 - 20 = 5P + 3P$$  
     $$100 = 8P$$  
   - Divide both sides by 8:  
     $$P = \frac{100}{8} = 12.5$$  

4. **Find the equilibrium quantity** by plugging $P = 12.5$ into either the demand or supply equation (both give the same result). Using supply:  
   $$Q_s = 20 + 3(12.5) = 20 + 37.5 = 57.5$$  

**Answer:** The new equilibrium price is **$12.5** and the equilibrium quantity is **57.5 units**. Because the demand curve shifted right, both price and quantity are higher than before the income increase.

### Summary of the mechanics

- **Movement**: Only price changes → use the same equation, plug in the new price, read the new quantity.  
- **Shift**: A non‑price factor changes → first rewrite the equation to reflect the new intercept or slope, then solve for the new equilibrium as we did above.

> **Remember:** When a curve shifts, the whole relationship between price and quantity changes. When we move along a curve, the relationship stays the same; only the price we are looking at is different.

Understanding this distinction lets you answer questions like: *Will a tax on producers raise the price buyers pay?* (It shifts supply left, then we find a new equilibrium.) Or *What happens if a popular new smartphone model drops in price?* (That is a movement along the demand curve.) By keeping the two ideas separate, you can analyze any market change clearly and correctly.

sections.heading: 7. Real‑World Application: Policy Impact
sections.body:
When a government changes the rules of the market, the ideas of supply, demand, and equilibrium help us see who really feels the impact.  
Two common tools are **taxes** (money the seller must pay to the government) and **subsidies** (money the government gives to the buyer).  
Both shift the cost that participants face, so the price that buyers pay and the price that sellers receive are no longer the same.

> **Definition:** *Tax on sellers* – a compulsory payment per unit sold that the seller must send to the government. It raises the seller’s cost of each unit.  
> **Definition:** *Subsidy to buyers* – a payment per unit that the government gives to the buyer, effectively lowering the price the buyer pays out‑of‑pocket.

Why does this matter?  
If we know the original supply and demand curves, we can predict the new equilibrium after the policy change. This tells us how much of the good will be bought and sold, and who bears the burden of the tax or enjoys the benefit of the subsidy.

### Step‑by‑step for a tax on sellers  

Suppose the original market is described by  

- Demand: $Q_D = 20 - 2P$  
- Supply: $Q_S = 4P$

where $Q$ is quantity (units) and $P$ is price (dollars).  
Without any tax, set $Q_D = Q_S$ to find the equilibrium:

$$20 - 2P = 4P \;\Longrightarrow\; 20 = 6P \;\Longrightarrow\; P^{*}= \frac{20}{6}\approx 3.33$$  
$$Q^{*}=4P^{*}=4(3.33)\approx 13.33$$  

Now the government imposes a **$2 tax on sellers**. The seller must pay $2 for every unit sold, so the price the seller receives, call it $P_S$, is $2 less than the price the buyer pays, $P_B$:

$$P_S = P_B - 2$$  

The supply curve expressed in terms of the buyer’s price becomes:

$$Q_S = 4P_S = 4(P_B-2) = 4P_B - 8$$  

The demand curve stays the same because buyers do not face the tax directly.

**Example 8 (Hard): Tax on sellers**  
*Impose a $2 tax on sellers in the original supply equation and determine the new equilibrium price paid by buyers and received by sellers.*

1. **Write the new supply equation in terms of the buyer’s price.**  
   $$Q_S = 4(P_B-2) = 4P_B - 8$$
2. **Set the new supply equal to demand and solve for the buyer’s price.**  
   $$20 - 2P_B = 4P_B - 8$$  
   $$20 + 8 = 6P_B$$  
   $$28 = 6P_B \;\Longrightarrow\; P_B = \frac{28}{6}\approx 4.67$$
3. **Find the price the seller actually receives** (subtract the tax).  
   $$P_S = P_B - 2 = 4.67 - 2 = 2.67$$  
   **Find the new quantity** by plugging $P_B$ into either equation.  
   $$Q = 20 - 2(4.67) = 20 - 9.33 = 10.67$$  

**Answer:** After the $2 tax, buyers pay about **$4.67** per unit, sellers receive about **$2.67**, and the market trades **10.7 units**. The tax reduces the quantity sold compared with the original 13.3 units.

> **Note:** The tax creates a *gap* between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. This gap is the tax amount, and the size of the gap shows who bears more of the burden. In this example, buyers pay $1.34 more than before, while sellers receive $0.66 less.

### Step‑by‑step for a subsidy to buyers  

Now keep the original curves but give the government a **$1 subsidy to each buyer**. The buyer’s effective price after the subsidy, $P_B^{\text{eff}}$, is the market price $P$ minus the subsidy:

$$P_B^{\text{eff}} = P - 1$$  

Because the buyer feels the good is cheaper by $1, the demand curve shifts outward (to the right). In terms of the market price $P$, the new demand relation is:

$$Q_D = 20 - 2(P - 1) = 20 - 2P + 2 = 22 - 2P$$  

Supply is unchanged: $Q_S = 4P$.

**Example 9 (Hard): Subsidy to buyers**  
*Give a $1 subsidy to buyers and compute the resulting equilibrium.*

1. **Write the shifted demand equation in terms of the market price.**  
   $$Q_D = 22 - 2P$$
2. **Set the new demand equal to supply and solve for the market price.**  
   $$22 - 2P = 4P$$  
   $$22 = 6P$$  
   $$P = \frac{22}{6}\approx 3.67$$
3. **Determine the effective price paid by buyers** (subtract the subsidy).  
   $$P_B^{\text{eff}} = 3.67 - 1 = 2.67$$  
   **Find the new quantity** using either curve.  
   $$Q = 4P = 4(3.67) = 14.68$$  

**Answer:** With a $1 buyer subsidy, the market price is about **$3.67**, buyers actually pay **$2.67**, sellers receive **$3.67**, and the market trades **14.7 units**. The subsidy raises the quantity traded compared with the original 13.3 units.

> **In daily life:** Think of a tax on soda as the government adding a $0.10 charge per can that the store must pay. The store raises its shelf price, so you end up paying more. A subsidy is like a coupon the government gives you for each kilogram of vegetables you buy; you see a lower price at checkout, and farmers may sell more because demand rises.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming the tax or subsidy changes only one side of the market. In reality, a seller tax shifts the supply curve, while a buyer subsidy shifts the demand curve. Forgetting which curve moves leads to the wrong equilibrium.

By following these steps—rewrite the affected curve, set it equal to the unchanged curve, solve for price, then compute quantity—you can evaluate any policy that changes the cost or benefit of buying or selling. This systematic approach lets economists predict the real‑world impact of taxes, subsidies, price controls, or other interventions.

practice.q: What does the law of demand say about the relationship between price and quantity demanded?
practice.a: The law of demand states that, all else equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. This inverse relationship is because higher prices discourage buyers, while lower prices encourage them.

practice.q: Explain why a surplus occurs in a market.
practice.a: A surplus happens when the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at a given price. Sellers have more of the good than buyers want to purchase, so unsold items accumulate. This usually pushes the price down as sellers try to attract more buyers.

practice.q: Compare a movement along the demand curve with a shift of the demand curve. Give one example of each.
practice.a: A movement along the demand curve is caused by a change in the good’s own price; for example, if the price of apples falls, the quantity demanded moves from point A to point B on the same curve. A shift of the demand curve occurs when something other than the price changes, such as consumer income. If incomes rise, the entire demand curve for apples shifts right, meaning at every price consumers now want to buy more apples.

practice.q: Describe how a price ceiling set below the equilibrium price creates a shortage, using the concepts of supply and demand.
practice.a: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. If it is set below the market‑clearing (equilibrium) price, the ceiling makes the good cheaper than what the market would normally charge. At this lower price, quantity demanded rises (because buyers want more of the cheaper good) while quantity supplied falls (because producers are less willing to sell at the lower price). The result is that demand exceeds supply, creating a shortage.

practice.q: A new tax on sugary drinks is expected to reduce consumption. Explain, using supply and demand curves, how the tax affects equilibrium price, quantity, and generates government revenue.
practice.a: The tax raises the cost of producing or selling sugary drinks, shifting the supply curve left (upward). The new supply curve intersects the original demand curve at a higher price and lower quantity. The price consumers pay rises to the new equilibrium price; the price producers receive is the equilibrium price minus the tax. Quantity sold falls, reflecting reduced consumption. Government revenue equals the tax amount multiplied by the new, lower quantity sold.

practice.q: Analyze how a sudden increase in consumer confidence might affect the market for smartphones, specifying the expected changes in demand, equilibrium price, and quantity, and explain why supply does not shift in the short run.
practice.a: Higher consumer confidence makes people feel richer, so they are willing to buy more smartphones at any given price. This shifts the demand curve rightward. The new intersection with the unchanged short‑run supply curve leads to a higher equilibrium price and a larger equilibrium quantity. Supply does not shift immediately because producers cannot instantly change production capacity, labor, or input inventories; those adjustments take time, so the supply curve stays the same in the short run.

data.recap: The lesson explains how price changes affect the quantities buyers want and sellers offer, describing the laws of demand and supply. It shows how to draw demand and supply curves, find market equilibrium, and understand shortages and surpluses. It also distinguishes movements along curves from shifts caused by other factors, and applies these ideas to taxes and subsidies.
